$comment: GOLDEN FIXTURES — this file is the spec (PLAN.md §4).
Each case: the URL, the verdict the engine must return, and the check ids that must fire.
Rules: never reference a live malicious URL. Craft examples, or use RFC 2606 / RFC 5737
reserved names (example.com, .invalid, .test, 192.0.2.0/24) so nothing here can ever resolve
`signals` is a subset assertion, not an exact set — a case may legitimately trip more checks
than it names. Where the exact set matters, the test file asserts it separately.

cases.note: Plain HTTPS, nothing fires. The baseline the whole product rests on.
One subdomain is ordinary depth.

Multi-part suffix: registrable must be example.co.uk, not co.uk.
Known hosting suffix — github.io is the public suffix, so depth is zero.
Bundled known-safe domain short-circuits.
A brand on its own subdomain is the real thing — deceptive-subdomain must stay silent.
User allowlist entry behaves like the bundled list.
Developer traffic. http still flags, but ip-host and nonstandard-port must not.
Router admin page on the private range — ip-host is exempt and http on a non-credential path is below threshold.
Unencrypted sign-in. Escalated because the path asks for credentials.
Sign-in page on an odd port.
Five levels of padding before the real domain.
Shortener. Destination unknown, not necessarily bad — must never read danger alone.

Top-tier: the TLD collides with a filename extension.
Open-redirect shape — a second address hidden in the query.
The @ hides the real host. Everything before it is discarded by the browser.
Credential page on a bare documentation-range IP, unencrypted.
Brand sits in the subdomain; the real owner is secure-billing.invalid.
rn reads as m at UI sizes. Folded to distance zero, so it is intent, not a typo.
Digit-for-letter homoglyph against a real brand.

Visible text names a different site than the href.
Bundled blocklist hit. Decisive on its own.
Blocklist matching covers subdomains, so one entry covers every host they spin up.
On both lists: the blocklist wins. Over-warning costs a click, under-warning costs an account.

An InertLink: the standard placeholder for a JS-driven control. Amazon's cart has fourteen of these (Search, Cart, Orders, 'See more categories'). Flagging them was the worst false positive in the project — no destination, so no verdict.
Attacker-authored document rendered inline.
Everything at once. Signals stack rather than short-circuit.
Unparseable. Never safe (ADR-0006).

Out of scope. We do not guess at schemes we do not model.
In-page anchor with no page context — nothing to evaluate.
Relative href resolved against the page. Resolution is string-only — never a fetch (golden rule 3).
javascript: with a real body. Runs in the page's own origin, which the site already controls — worth checking, not an emergency.
How ordinary sites hand you a generated file. Flagging every download button was a false positive with no threat behind it.
